title: Commercial insurance outlook for 2027: the good and the bad in P&C insurance market trends
summary: Commercial insurance outlook for 2027: property softens, casualty stays firm and premium per submission falls 12%. What it means for your margin.
body_markdown:
The commercial insurance outlook for 2027 is good on profit and bad on direction, because the market will pay carriers less for each submission while casualty claims ask more of every decision. According to[AM Best's 2025 results review, reported by Carrier Management in July 2026](https://www.carriermanagement.com/news/2026/07/17/290139.htm) , the US P&C industry closed 2025 at a 93 combined ratio, its best underwriting result in a decade, and commercial lines underwriting income more than doubled to $19.2B. That cushion is real, and it is already thinning. AM Best expects the commercial lines combined ratio to rise to 96.3 in 2026 from 95.8 in 2025, according to its[2026 market segment outlook](https://www.insurancejournal.com/magazines/mag-features/2026/03/09/860644.htm) , while the CIAB reported that average commercial premiums fell 2% in the second quarter of 2026. Read together, these P&C insurance market trends point to one conclusion for a chief underwriting officer: rate will do less of the work in 2027, so the combined ratio will be decided inside the underwriting operation, in what it costs to clear each submission and how accurately each casualty account is selected and priced.


## What does the commercial insurance outlook for 2027 look like?


The 2027 market is two markets running in opposite directions at the same time. Property pricing keeps falling while casualty pricing stays firm, and most commercial, specialty and E&S books carry both. According to the[CIAB's Q2 2026 market survey, reported by Insurance Journal in August 2026](https://insurancejournal.com/news/national/2026/08/20/882240.htm) , commercial property premiums fell 6.3% on average, the largest decrease of any line, while umbrella rose 5.3% for a 35th consecutive quarter and commercial auto rose 4.5%. WTW's[Insurance Marketplace Realities 2027 report](https://www.agencyequity.com/articles/commercial-insurance-market-becomes-more-favorable-for-buyers-heading-into-2027) describes a market that is largely favorable for buyers heading into 2027, with large and complex property programs down 14.5% on average in the second quarter and excess casualty increases nearing their peak as new capacity arrives. The Swiss Re Institute's[sigma report from June 2026](https://www.swissre.com/institute/research/sigma-research/sigma-2026-07-world-insurance/insurance-stabilising-force-cycle-softens.html) expects commercial pricing to stay soft through 2027, supported by strong profits and ample capital. The table below lays out the line-by-line picture for an underwriting leader's 2027 plan.


Line Latest rate signal 2027 direction What it means for underwriting


**Commercial property** -6.3% in Q2 2026 (CIAB); large, complex programs -14.5% (WTW) More decreases at a slower pace Exposure and valuation data decide who keeps margin as rate falls


**Umbrella and excess** +5.3% in Q2 2026, 35th straight rise (CIAB) Increases near their peak (WTW) Prior-loss and attachment accuracy matter more as rate gains slow


**Commercial auto** +4.5% in Q2 2026 (CIAB); $1.9B underwriting loss in 2025 (AM Best) Firm Fleet and driver data errors price straight into the combined ratio


**General liability** Low single-digit primary increases (Business Insurance, Oct 2026) Firm and severity-led Rate roughly keeps pace with loss trend, so selection carries the margin


**Workers' compensation** -3.2% in Q2 2026 (CIAB) Among the steadiest casualty lines (WTW) Margin comes from handling small accounts at low cost


**Cyber** -3.2% in Q2 2026 (CIAB) Between -5% and +5% (WTW) Flat pricing rewards a sharper controls review at intake


**E&S overall** Premium +2.8% and items +16.9% in H1 2026 (WSIA) More flow, thinner premium per item Throughput per premium dollar becomes the core operating metric


## What is good about the 2027 market for carriers and MGAs?


The good news is that most carriers enter 2027 with real profit, real capacity and a wider pool of business. A soft market that starts from a strong position gives an underwriting leader time to fix the operation before margins compress, which is a luxury the last soft market did not offer. Four things work in a carrier's favor heading into the year:


- **A profit cushion.** Commercial lines underwriting income more than doubled to $19.2B in 2025, according to AM Best, and commercial auto's underwriting loss narrowed to about $1.9B from $4.9B a year earlier.
- **Ample capital and capacity.** The Swiss Re Institute expects pricing to stay soft through 2027 because profitability is strong and capital is plentiful, which keeps capacity available for carriers and MGAs that want to grow in their best classes.
- **A wider pool of submissions.** According to the[WSIA midyear report, covered by Business Insurance in August 2026](https://www.businessinsurance.com/surplus-lines-premium-growth-slows-sharply-in-first-half-of-2026/) , surplus lines item filings rose 16.9% to 4.28 million in the first half of 2026, so E&S writers see more of the market than ever before.
- **Stable workers' compensation.** WTW describes workers' compensation as one of the steadier casualty lines, which gives multi-line books a dependable earnings base while other lines move.


The opportunity inside that list is selection. A carrier that sees 17% more submissions without adding underwriters can quote the accounts that fit its appetite first, and in a soft market the best accounts go to whoever answers the broker soonest with a firm, well-priced quote.


## What is bad about the 2027 market for underwriting margins?


The bad news is that casualty claims keep rising faster than casualty rate in the lines that already lose money. According to AM Best, the other liability occurrence line ran a 114.7 combined ratio in 2025, an improvement on 120.3 that still left an underwriting loss of about $11B. BCG's[2026 Insurance Value Creators report](https://www.bcg.com/publications/2026/soft-rates-and-big-risks-reshape-the-us-p-and-c-market) counts $62B of adverse development in commercial liability between 2015 and 2024 and a record 135 nuclear verdicts in 2024, which means reserves set years ago are still catching up with today's courtrooms. Our earlier look at[social inflation in 2027](https://www.pibit.ai/blog/social-inflation-2027-casualty-outlook) covers that severity trend in depth. Three more pressures sit on top of it:


- **Property rate falls fastest where profit was highest.** Property carried many books through the last two years, and the Swiss Re Institute expects US rebuilding costs to run 7% higher by 2027, so falling rate meets rising replacement cost on the same schedule.
- **Returns are past their peak.** The Swiss Re Institute puts global non-life return on equity at 11.4% for 2026, down from a 14% peak in 2025.
- **Each submission brings in less premium.** Surplus lines premium grew 2.8% in the first half of 2026 while filings grew 16.9%, according to the WSIA, so the average premium per filing fell by about 12%.


## Why will premium per submission decide 2027 margins?


Premium per submission decides 2027 margins because most underwriting costs scale with submission count, while revenue scales with premium. Working from the WSIA figures, the average surplus lines filing carried about $12,647 of premium in the first half of 2025 and about $11,121 in the first half of 2026, a drop of roughly 12%. An underwriting team still has to clear, read, research and triage every one of those filings, whether it binds or not, so the cost of handling a submission stays put while the premium it can earn shrinks. The illustration below shows what that does to a $500M book where intake, research and triage cost the equivalent of 6 points of premium today.


Illustrative $500M book 2025 pattern 2027 pattern


Average premium per submission (WSIA E&S proxy) $12,647 $11,121 (about 12% lower)


Intake, research and triage cost per submission Unchanged Unchanged


That cost as a share of premium 6.0 points 6.8 points


**Effect on the combined ratio** Baseline **+0.8 points, about $4.1M of underwriting profit**


That 0.8-point drift is larger than the half-point rise AM Best projects for the whole commercial segment in 2026, and it arrives before a single claim is paid. The[combined ratio](https://www.pibit.ai/insurance-knowledge/combined-ratio) has two halves, and in 2027 the expense half moves first. We made the same throughput argument for surplus lines in our piece on[E&S submission volume in a soft market](https://www.pibit.ai/blog/es-submission-volume-soft-rates-throughput-problem) , and the 2027 outlook extends it to admitted commercial books as property rate keeps falling.


## Where should a CUO put underwriting effort in 2027?


A CUO should spend 2027 effort where the market no longer helps: cost per submission on the soft lines and decision accuracy on the hard ones. Rate softening was the theme of our[2026 rate softening analysis](https://www.pibit.ai/blog/commercial-pc-rate-softening-2026-underwriting-automation) , and the 2027 picture adds the casualty severity problem on top of it. Four moves follow from the outlook:


- **Clear and rank every submission on day one.** Appetite checks, duplicate checks and completeness checks should run before an underwriter opens the file, so senior time goes only to accounts the carrier can win and wants to write.
- **Verify the casualty fields that drive severity.** Prior losses, venue, fleet size, driver records and attachment points carry the most weight in umbrella, auto and general liability pricing, so each of these values should be checked against its source document before it reaches the rater.
- **Protect property margin with better exposure data.** When rate falls and rebuilding costs rise, the gap between a stated value and a real one becomes the margin, so valuation and location data deserve the same scrutiny casualty data gets.
- **Measure the operation in premium terms.** Track cost per submission against premium per submission by line, and treat a widening gap as an early warning for the combined ratio.


Each of these moves frees underwriter capacity, which matters because the talent pool is not growing as fast as submission flow. Our guide to[growing GWP without growing headcount](https://www.pibit.ai/blog/underwriter-capacity-commercial-pc-grow-gwp-2026-soft-market) covers the capacity side of the same plan.
